title: The Box That Sings
blurb: Six strings, a hollow box, and some very old math. How a guitar turns the shiver of a wire into a sound you can feel.

blocks.text: This is a guitar. It is a wooden box with strings. Pull a string and let it go. The string shakes. It shakes so fast you cannot see it. The shaking makes a sound. blocks.prompt: The Box That Sings
blocks.text: A guitar has six strings. Each one is a different size. When you pluck a string, it shakes back and forth very fast. That shaking is called a vibration. The vibration travels down the string and into the wood. The flat front of the guitar is thin, like a drum skin. It shakes too. It pushes on the air, and the air carries the sound to your ears. A thick, loose string shakes slowly and makes a low sound. A thin, tight string shakes quickly and makes a high sound. Press a string against the neck and you make it shorter. Short strings sing higher.

answers: six
a vibration
a thick, loose string

3.title: The Box That Sings
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: How a Guitar Gets Loud
blocks.text: Pluck a guitar string on its own, stretched between two nails, and you will barely hear it. A string is thin. It slices through the air instead of pushing it. Almost no sound gets out. Now stretch that same string across a guitar. The string still shakes, but now the shaking runs down through a little wooden bar called the bridge and into the flat front of the guitar, which is called the soundboard. The soundboard is wide and thin, and it shakes along with the string. A wide surface can shove a lot of air at once. That is what your ears hear. The hole matters too. The body is a box of trapped air, and when the soundboard pumps, the air inside bounces in and out of the hole and adds a deep boom to the low notes. The neck is covered in metal ridges called frets. Press a string just behind a fret and you shorten the part that can shake. Shorter means faster. Faster means higher. The frets are not spaced evenly. Each one sits a little closer to the last, because the math of pitch works that way.

4.title: The Box That Sings
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The top is often under three millimeters of spruce
Six strings pull with over 150 pounds of force
The hidden struts underneath are called bracing
Antonio de Torres, Spain, the 1850s
He built one with a papier mache body to prove a point

blocks.prompt: The Skeleton You Never See
blocks.text: A guitar is a machine built around one stubborn problem. To make sound, the front of the instrument has to be thin. A thick top is stiff, and a stiff top will not vibrate, and a top that will not vibrate is silent. So the soundboard on a good acoustic guitar is often less than three millimeters of spruce, thinner than two coins stacked together. Here is the problem. The six strings of a steel-string guitar pull on that thin top with a combined force of over one hundred and fifty pounds, about the weight of a grown adult, and they never stop pulling. Left alone, a sheet of wood that thin would fold up like paper. The answer is bracing. Underneath the soundboard, hidden where nobody looks, a builder glues a skeleton of narrow wooden struts. Struts standing on edge are astonishingly strong for their weight, which is why bridges and floors use the same trick. The bracing holds the top flat against years of pulling while adding almost no weight, so the top stays light enough to sing. In the 1850s, a Spanish builder named Antonio de Torres arranged those struts in a fan, spreading them out from under the bridge toward the bottom of the box. He also made the body bigger. His guitars were louder and richer than anything before them, and nearly every acoustic guitar since has copied his plan. Torres knew exactly what he had done. He once built a guitar with a body of papier mache, everything except the top and the bracing, to prove where the sound really came from. It worked. It played.

5.title: The Box That Sings
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A pickup is a magnet wrapped in fine wire
It reads the string, not the air
The Frying Pan, about 1932

blocks.prompt: The Guitar That Gave Up on Air
blocks.text: An acoustic guitar is a machine for moving air. Everything about it, the thin spruce top, the hidden bracing, the hollow box, exists to take the tiny shiver of a steel string and turn it into a pressure wave big enough to reach the back of a room. It is an elegant machine, and by the 1920s it had run out of room. The problem was the dance band. Guitarists sat in orchestras next to trumpets, saxophones, and drum kits, and they simply could not be heard. The guitar was a rhythm instrument by default, chopping out chords in the background, because no matter how hard you hit it, a wooden box can only shove so much air. The solution abandoned air entirely. In the early 1930s, George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker built and sold an instrument nicknamed the Frying Pan, and it worked on a principle Michael Faraday had described a century earlier. Wrap thousands of turns of fine wire around a magnet and hold it under a steel string. The magnet turns the string itself into a magnet. When the string vibrates, the magnetic field around the coil changes, and a changing magnetic field pushes a current through wire. That current is an electrical copy of the string's motion, and you can send it down a cable to an amplifier and make it as loud as you like. Notice what is gone. The pickup does not listen to the sound of the guitar. It has no microphone. It ignores the air, the room, the wood, and the audience, and reads the string directly. Once you understand that, the solid-body electric guitar stops looking strange. If the body is not making the sound, it does not need to be hollow, and a hollow body was actually causing trouble, howling with feedback in front of a loud amplifier. Leo Fender's solid-body, which went on sale in 1950 and soon took the name Telecaster, was essentially a plank of ash with a bolted-on neck. Critics called it a canoe paddle. It did not feed back, it stayed in tune, it sustained notes far longer than any acoustic, and a factory could turn one out in pieces. The guitar had spent four hundred years getting quietly better at pushing air. In twenty years it stopped trying, and became the loudest instrument on the stage.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The frets crowd together as they near the body
Each fret leaves about 94.4 percent of the string
The twelfth root of two is roughly 1.0595
The 12th fret halves the string and doubles the pitch
The old shortcut: the rule of eighteen
Equal temperament: twelve equal steps per octave

blocks.prompt: The Ruler Made of Math
blocks.text: Look closely at the neck of a guitar and you will notice something that seems like a mistake. The metal frets are not evenly spaced. Down by the tuning pegs they sit far apart, wide enough to stretch a hand across. As they march toward the body they crowd together, until near the end they are packed so tightly that a fingertip barely fits between them. Every guitar ever built has this same crowding, and every one crowds by exactly the same amounts. That is not a style choice. It is arithmetic, made visible in metal and wood. Start with the string. A stretched string vibrates at a rate set mostly by three things: how long it is, how tight it is, and how heavy it is. Tuning pegs adjust the tightness. String makers control the weight. The frets control the length, and length is the one you change while you play. Press a string down just behind a fret and the vibrating part now runs only from that fret to the bridge. It is shorter, so it vibrates faster, so the note is higher. Now the crucial fact, known to the Greeks and probably long before them: halve the length of a string and you exactly double its frequency. That doubling is the interval we call an octave, and it is the most agreeable sound in music, so agreeable that we give both notes the same name. This is why the twelfth fret sits at the precise midpoint of the string. Everything else follows from deciding how to divide up the space between one note and its octave. For centuries, Western musicians divided it using tidy whole-number ratios, which sound gorgeous in one key and increasingly sour as you move away from it. A tuning that flatters music in C betrays music in F sharp. Keyboard players simply avoided the bad keys. Guitarists could not, because the frets are fixed bars that cross every string at once. The compromise that won is called equal temperament. Split the octave into twelve steps that are all the same size, and accept that almost none of them is perfectly in tune with the old ratios. In exchange, every key sounds equally slightly wrong, which is to say every key becomes usable. To build it, each fret has to raise the pitch by the same multiple. That multiple is the twelfth root of two, roughly 1.0595, because twelve of them multiplied together give exactly two, which is the octave. Run that backward and you get a rule for cutting fret slots. Each fret shortens the remaining string to about 94.4 percent of what was left before it. Since each fret takes its share of a smaller and smaller remainder, the gaps shrink as you go. Luthiers once did this with a formula known as the rule of eighteen, dividing the remaining length by roughly 17.817 and marking off that distance. Modern builders use the exact figure, but the shape of the answer never changes, which is why frets always crowd toward the body. So the fingerboard is not merely a place to put your fingers. It is a physical printout of a mathematical argument that took Western music several hundred years to finish having. Every guitarist, without needing to know any of it, plays a compromise with their hands.
